original_question: Is it consistent that the almost-disjointness number a equals the splitting number s and yet every 2-coloring of a×ω has a monochromatic rectangle of sizes a and ω, that is, \( inom{a}{\omega} 	o  inom{a}{\omega}^{1,1}_2\)?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 3.17: the paper asks whether it is consistent that the almost-disjointness number equals the splitting number and simultaneously the strong polarized relation \binom{\mathfrak a}{\omega} \to \binom{\mathfrak a}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 holds. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target: it uses the right invariants (\mathfrak a and \mathfrak s), the right consistency form, the right pair (\mathfrak a,\omega), and it correctly paraphrases the strong polarized relation as saying that every 2-coloring of \mathfrak a\times\omega has a monochromatic rectangle whose sides have sizes \mathfrak a and \omega. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
missing_details: It should say explicitly that this is a consistency question over ZFC, e.g. 'Is there a model of ZFC in which ... ?' The paper phrases it exactly as 'Is it consistent that ... ?' in Problem 3.17. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))

To make the question stand-alone, define \mathfrak a as the least cardinality of a maximal almost disjoint family of infinite subsets of \omega, and define \mathfrak s as the least cardinality of a splitting family in [\omega]^\omega. The paper's Problem 3.17 uses only the symbols a and s and relies on standard background on cardinal invariants. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))

The arrow notation should be unpacked exactly as in Definition 1.1: \binom{\lambda}{\kappa}\to\binom{\lambda}{\kappa}^{1,1}_2 means that for every coloring c:\lambda\times\kappa\to 2 there are A\subseteq\lambda and B\subseteq\kappa with |A|=\lambda and |B|=\kappa such that c\upharpoonright(A\times B) is constant. Specializing to (\lambda,\kappa)=(\mathfrak a,\omega) yields the precise formulation here. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))

For full set-theoretic precision, the domain \mathfrak a\times\omega should be understood in the standard way as the product of the initial ordinals/cardinals representing those cardinals; the paper's notation assumes this convention. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))

The nearby context shows why this question is asked: after Theorem 2.6, the paper has positive results below the relevant splitting threshold, and then Problem 3.17 asks whether one can still have a positive relation exactly at the boundary where \mathfrak a=\mathfrak s. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
refined_question: Is there a model of ZFC in which \mathfrak a=\mathfrak s, where \mathfrak a is the least size of a maximal almost disjoint family of infinite subsets of \omega and \mathfrak s is the splitting number, and such that for every coloring c:\mathfrak a\times\omega\to 2 there exist A\subseteq\mathfrak a and B\subseteq\omega with |A|=\mathfrak a and |B|=\omega for which c\upharpoonright(A\times B) is constant? ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, is it consistent that \mathfrak a=\mathfrak s and \binom{\mathfrak a}{\omega}\to\binom{\mathfrak a}{\omega}^{1,1}_2? This equivalence is exactly the content of Definition 1.1 specialized to (\lambda,\kappa)=(\mathfrak a,\omega). ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Section 3, Problem 3.17, and your draft is essentially a faithful paraphrase of it. Definition 1.1 supplies the exact meaning of the partition arrow notation, so the only real refinement needed is to make the cardinal-invariant symbols explicit and to state the quantifiers in full. The nearby discussion after Problem 3.16, together with Theorem 2.6 from the background section, explains the paper's intent: the splitting number largely controls the positive spectrum, and the open point here is whether a positive strong polarized relation can persist right at the boundary where \mathfrak a meets \mathfrak s. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/95093/1012.pdf))
